findings.where: Screen 11 (Decibels), and the dB puzzles on screens 12 and 13
findings.what: The screen states "the decibels of a power ratio are ten times its log" as plain fact, but neither of the lesson's two sources quotes that definition (the LibreTexts quote covers only multiplying becoming adding), the decibel self-check has no source, and the 10 is listed as a cited constant; add the ITU or Britannica definition the brief names (notes 4.10) as a source, or word the screen "Textbooks define ..." as the explain text does.

Only the product law is written as a formula, while the quotient and power laws appear only in words ("Taking away divides, a power multiplies a length"); set log(ab) = log a + log b, log(a ÷ b) = log a − log b and log(aⁿ) = n log a side by side so he can say all three back (MCA: "States laws of logarithms"), and give "Taking away" its subject (one length from another) so it does not read like the "divide means subtract" slogan the brief bans.

The text jumps from "how many 2s multiply to make 5" to "how many lengths of log 2 fit into log 5" without saying why; add the link from screen 7, that 2 to a power x sits x lengths of log 2 along, which the explain text has but the screen does not.

In a steps lesson the screens are the whole lesson, yet 20 log for a voltage ratio (a point the brief requires, with its "10 or 20" check) and a loss as negative decibels (a cable halving the power is about −3 dB) appear only in the explain and practice text; voltage gain is the usual case in electro-technology, so add one line to screen 11 or to screen 13's Why.

findings.where: Screens 3 and 11 (brief items not on screen)
findings.what: Three points the brief promised are not on any screen: the laws need one base throughout; the log of any base is 1 (shown only as log 10 = 1, not log₂ 2 = 1 or ln e = 1); and the engine-room readings in dB(A) from IMO, which appear only in the "ignores" note.

The answer, 2, is read where the top ruler's 1 sits, but unlike screens 6 and 14 this screen has no tag marking it; also, once the demonstration ends, dragging the top ruler carries the cursor with it, so Dan cannot repeat the move he just watched (cursor held on 6 while the ruler slides).

The lead sentence plus an 85-word step text push the rulers about 570 px down the frame, so the 4-second demonstration may finish before Dan scrolls to it (Play again rescues it); drop the lead, which repeats the step's first sentence, and trim screens 1, 3 and 11, each about 90 words.

The rulers open aligned at 1 with the cursor lying on their left edges and its tags crowded into the corner, so the cursor is hard to see for the first half second, and the rows kept for the bars and bracket leave about 100 px of blank space under the rulers until the demonstration fills them.

Labels are 13 viewBox units, which comes to about 10.7 px on a 360 px phone, where the drawing is about 280 px wide; they are legible in the light and dark captures but small, and at 1280 px the rulers stay at 352 px in a wide column, so consider larger labels on phones or a wider drawing on desktop.

It says a decibel reading sits under the readout on every screen and that 40 and 50 are numbered on the bottom ruler; in fact the decibel line appears only on the decibel screens, 50 is only a tick (BOT_N stops at 40), and 40 is crowded out by 30 at 360 px, so its label never shows except as a tag.
